title: Passing a structure to a function: copy, reference or pointer

visuals.title: Copy, same box, or address: three ways to pass a Student

steps.note: main has the variable a at address 0x1000.
By value: a NEW Student box (0x2000) is made and the whole of a is copied into it.
Only the copy changes. a is still {Ali, 60}.
The function ends. The copy is destroyed, so the bonus is lost.
By reference: no new box. The parameter s is just another name for a at 0x1000.
This changes a itself, because s and a are the same box.
By pointer: p stores the ADDRESS of a (0x1000). Only 4 or 8 bytes are copied, not the whole Student.
The arrow follows the pointer to a and changes it.

visuals.title: Match each way of passing to what it does

pairs.meaning: By value: a full copy is made; changes are lost
By reference: the same box; changes stay in the caller's variable
By const reference: no copy and no changes allowed; best for read-only
By pointer: the address is passed; use p->marks to reach members
Same as (*p).marks: member of the structure that p points to
The caller passes the variable normally; the & appears only in the function header

goal: After this you can pass a structure to a function by value, by reference, by const reference and by pointer, use the arrow operator, and choose the right way for each job.
warmup: A student gives a form to the office. Option 1: the clerk makes a photocopy and writes remarks on the copy; the original stays clean. Option 2: the clerk gets the original form and writes on it. Option 3: the clerk may read the original but is not allowed to write anything. Option 4: the clerk is only told on which shelf the form is kept. A structure travelling into a function has exactly these four options.
definition: A structure variable can be sent to a function like any other variable. By value (void f(Student s)): the function gets a full copy of every member, so changes are lost when it returns. By reference (void f(Student &s)): s is another name for the caller's variable, so changes stay. By const reference (void f(const Student &s)): like a reference, but the function promises not to change it, and no copy is made. By pointer (void f(Student *p)): the function receives the address of the variable. Through a pointer we reach members with the arrow operator: p->marks, which means the same as (*p).marks.
howItWorks: Step through the first trace and watch the call stack. In bonusByValue the function gets a NEW box s filled with a copy of a. It adds 5 to the copy, and when the function ends the copy is thrown away, so main still has 60. In bonusByRef no new box is made. s is the same box as a, so the 5 marks are added to a. The function show uses a const reference: it does not copy the structure, and the compiler stops us if we try to change it. Why not always pass by value? A structure may hold many members, so copying it every time is slow and wasteful. The third trace shows the pointer way: the function receives the address, so only a small address is copied, and the arrow -> follows it to the real structure. A simple rule: read only, use const Type &. Must change it, use Type &. Small struct and you want a private copy, by value is fine. Pointer: use it when the notes or the exam ask for it, or when the address may be missing.
syntax:
struct Student { string name; int marks; };

void f1(Student s)        { s.marks += 5; }    // by value: copy, change is lost
void f2(Student &s)       { s.marks += 5; }    // by reference: changes the original
void f3(const Student &s) { cout << s.marks; } // const reference: read only, no copy
void f4(Student *p)       { p->marks += 5; }   // pointer: arrow reaches the member

Student a = {"Ali", 60};
f1(a);      // a unchanged
f2(a);      // a changed
f3(a);      // just reads
f4(&a);     // pass the ADDRESS of a

worked.problem: A Student has a name and marks. Write one function that adds 5 bonus marks BY VALUE and one BY REFERENCE, and a function that prints. Show which bonus is kept.
pseudocode: CALL bonusByValue(a): the function adds 5 to a copy
CALL bonusByRef(a): the function adds 5 to a itself

sample.title: Bonus marks: by value, by reference, by const reference

explanation.text: A struct with a string and an int.
By value: s is a copy of the argument. The whole struct is copied, every member.
Changes the copy only. The caller's variable is untouched.
By reference: s is another name for the caller's variable. No copy.
Changes the original a, because s and a are the same box.
By const reference: no copy and the function may only read s. Good for printing.
One variable a lives in main.
Marks stay 60.
Marks become 65.

steps.note: The program starts at main().
main creates the structure variable a with name Ali and marks 60.
The parameter is plain Student s, so a NEW Student box s is made and the whole of a is COPIED into it. s is a different box from a.
Only the copy changes: s.marks becomes 65. a.marks is still 60.
The function returned and the copy was thrown away. The bonus is lost. show takes a const reference: no copy is made and it cannot change a.
show prints the ORIGINAL data: the bonus was lost.
The parameter is Student &s. No new box is made: s becomes another name for a.
s.marks is a.marks, so the original a now has 65.
show looks at a again (no copy).
This time the bonus is kept.
The program ends.

sample.title: Point: by value, by reference, by const reference

explanation.text: Two int members written in one line: x and y.
By value: p is a copy. Fine here because we only read it and Point is small.
By reference: the function must change the caller's point.
Changes the original point's x.
const reference: no copy and no change allowed. The best choice for read-only access.
x squared plus y squared, the squared distance from (0, 0).
a starts at (2, 3).
a becomes (7, 3).

sample.title: Passing the address of a structure: the arrow operator

explanation.text: p is a pointer to a Student. Only an address is copied, not the whole struct.
The arrow -> reaches a member through a pointer. p->marks is the same as (*p).marks.
A normal structure variable.
ptr stores the address of s.
Pass the address of s with &. The function changes the original.
Passing a pointer variable works the same way.
The long form: dereference first, then use the dot. The arrow is a shortcut for this.

steps.note: The program starts at main().
main creates s: name Sara, marks 70.
ptr is a pointer. It stores the address of s (written &s here), so it points to the whole structure.
&s is the address of s. The parameter p receives a COPY of that address, so p points to the same s. The struct itself is not copied.
p->marks means: go to the structure p points to and use its marks. That is s.marks, so it becomes 75.
Back in main, s really changed.
We can also pass the pointer variable itself. p again points to s.
s.marks becomes 80.
In main we use ptr->name and ptr->marks the same way.
(*ptr) means the structure itself, so (*ptr).marks is the same as ptr->marks.
The program ends.

variations.when: The structure is small and you want to work on a private copy, or you only read it.
variations.example: void show(Point p) { cout << p.x; }  // show(a);

variations.when: The function must change the caller's structure.
variations.example: void moveRight(Point &p, int d) { p.x += d; }  // moveRight(a, 5);

variations.way: By const reference: void f(const Student &s)
variations.when: The function only reads and the structure may be big (best for printing and calculating).
variations.example: double dist(const Point &p) { return p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y; }

variations.when: The notes or the question ask for an address, or you meet code written in the pointer style.
Dot after a variable, arrow after a pointer.
variations.example:
a.marks   // a is a variable
ptr->marks   // ptr is a pointer, same as (*ptr).marks

mistakes.error: No compiler error. The program runs but the bonus is lost because only a copy was changed. Forgetting & is the most common mistake here.
error: assignment of member 'Student::marks' in read-only object
error: request for member 'marks' in 'p', which is of pointer type 'Student*' (maybe you meant to use '->' ?)

examTips: Write the three headers side by side in the exam: (Student s) copy, (Student &s) same box, (const Student &s) read only. Say what happens to the caller's variable in each case.
If the question says the function must change the structure, you need & (or a pointer). If it only prints or calculates, use const &.
The call looks the same for by value and by reference: f(a). The difference is only in the function header. For a pointer you write f(&a).
Dot with a variable, arrow with a pointer. p->x is exactly (*p).x.
A const reference parameter cannot be assigned to. If the question shows an assignment inside such a function, that is the compile error.
romanSummary: Structure ko function mein teen-chaar tarah bhej sakte hain: by value (copy), by reference &, by const reference, aur pointer se.
By value mein function copy par kaam karta hai, is liye original nahi badalta.
By reference (Student &s) mein same box milta hai, is liye changes original mein reh jate hain.
Sirf parhna ho to const Student & best hai: copy bhi nahi banti aur change bhi nahi ho sakta.
Pointer ke saath member tak jane ke liye arrow use hota hai: p->marks, jo (*p).marks ke barabar hai.

practice.prompt: A function has the header void f(Student s). What happens when it changes s.marks?
options: Only the copy changes; the caller's variable stays the same
practice.answer: Only the copy changes; the caller's variable stays the same
practice.explanation: With a plain Student s parameter the function works on a copy, so the caller's variable is unchanged.

practice.hint: Is p a copy or the same box as a?
practice.explanation: p is a copy. Setting it to 99 does not touch a, so a.x is still 1.
p is the same box as a, so the swap changes a: x becomes 8 and y becomes 3.

practice.hint: A const reference cannot be changed.
practice.explanation: The function must change the structure, so the parameter must not be const.

practice.hint: p is a pointer, not a variable.
practice.explanation: With a pointer we use the arrow operator: p->marks (the same as (*p).marks).

practice.prompt: Write a struct Person with a string name and an int age, and a function birthday that adds 1 to the age of the person that main passes in.
practice.hint: The function must change the original.
practice.explanation: A reference parameter makes p the same box as the caller's Person, so p.age++ changes it.

practice.hint: Only two of the three functions can change x.
practice.explanation: f1 works on a copy (lost). f2 adds 10 and f3 adds 100 to the real x, so x.v = 110.

quiz.prompt: Which header lets the function change the caller's structure?
quiz.explanation: A plain reference is the same box as the caller's variable.

options: No copy is made and the function will not change s
s is deleted at the end
quiz.answer: No copy is made and the function will not change s
quiz.explanation: A const reference avoids the copy and forbids changes.

quiz.prompt: p is a pointer to a Student. How do you read its marks?
quiz.explanation: With a pointer use ->, which equals (*p).marks.

quiz.prompt: Why is passing a big structure by value often a poor choice?
options: The whole structure is copied every call
It makes the program print twice
quiz.answer: The whole structure is copied every call
quiz.explanation: Every member is copied each time, which wastes time and memory.

quiz.prompt: How do you call void bonus(Student *p) for a variable a?
quiz.explanation: The parameter is a pointer, so pass the address of a with &.
